open_obligations: Note that Leike et al. state an informal analogy, not a theorem.
Check that the user's binary evaluation plays the role of Irving et al.'s polynomial-time judge H.
Check whether assistance agents answering subquestions map onto adversarial quantifiers.

Note that Irving et al.'s Theorem 1 is about optimal play in the debate game, while Leike et al.'s agents A1 and A2 are trained on the user's evaluations and the cited passage makes no optimal-play assumption.
out.other_title: Theorem 1: debate with a polynomial-time judge and optimal play decides PSPACE
out.rationale: Irving et al. show n-round debate with a polynomial-time judge corresponds to formulas with alternating quantifiers (Sigma_n P for fixed n, PSPACE with polynomially many rounds). Leike et al. credit this analogy to Irving et al. and argue reward modeling resembles NP while recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers; no theorem is proved.
out.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the complexity-theory analogy between recursion depth in oversight schemes and alternating quantifiers

text: The authors argue, via an analogy to complexity theory first introduced by Irving et al. (2018), that recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers, e.g. A2 proposes behavior x, A1 responds with assisting behavior y, and the user evaluates both. With polynomially bounded quantifiers and a polynomial-time formula, reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems.
title: Complexity analogy: reward modeling ~ NP, recursion depth k ~ k alternating quantifiers
